title: Israeli criticism of his impartiality as ICJ President in cases concerning Israel
description: As a judge (from 2018) and President (from 6 February 2024) of the International Court of Justice, Salam sat in several proceedings involving parties in the region. In South Africa v. Israel, in which South Africa accuses Israel of genocide in Gaza and Israel rejects the accusation, he was a member of the bench for the provisional-measures order of 26 January 2024 and presided over the orders of 28 March 2024 (to which he appended a declaration) and 24 May 2024, which ordered Israel to halt its military offensive in Rafah. He presided over the hearings and read out the Court's advisory opinion of 19 July 2024, requested by the UN General Assembly, which found Israel's continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (the UN's term) unlawful and called for an end to settlement activity; he appended a declaration, and Israel's Foreign Ministry rejected the opinion as 'fundamentally wrong' while Prime Minister Netanyahu's office called it a 'decision of lies'. He also presided in Nicaragua v. Germany (an April 2024 order declining to indicate provisional measures over Germany's military and other support to Israel) and sat in Canada and the Netherlands v. Syria under the Convention against Torture (provisional measures ordered on 16 November 2023). UN Watch, a Geneva-based advocacy group, said in July 2024 that as Lebanon's UN ambassador he had voted 210 times to denounce Israel. On his appointment as Prime Minister in January 2025, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said Salam had 'called Israel an enemy' and that his 'decisions regarding Israel must be disqualified'. Salam is not a party to any of these cases, which are proceedings between states or advisory proceedings.
key_facts: 6 February 2024: elected ICJ President by his peers for three years (ICJ)
28 March and 24 May 2024: presided over orders in South Africa v. Israel; declaration appended to the March order
19 July 2024: read out the advisory opinion on Israel's policies in the Occupied Palestinian Territory; Israel rejected it
14 January 2025: Sa'ar says Salam's decisions regarding Israel must be disqualified
Salam resigned from the Court on 14 January 2025 and took no further part in these cases

title: Ban on Iranian flights, airport-road riots and attack on a UN convoy
description: About a week after Salam's government was formed, Lebanese authorities stopped Iranian aircraft from landing in Beirut after the Israeli military accused Iran of using civilian flights to bring cash to Hezbollah; according to The National the decision followed a US warning that Israel would attack the airport. Supporters said to be from Hezbollah blocked the airport road on consecutive days, and on 14 February 2025 protesters attacked a UNIFIL convoy, setting a vehicle on fire and wounding two people, including the force's outgoing deputy commander. Hezbollah's Al-Manar blamed 'unruly elements', Amal condemned the attack, and UNIFIL said attacks on peacekeepers 'may amount to war crimes'.
key_facts: Mid-February 2025: Iranian flights barred from landing in Beirut
14 February 2025: UNIFIL convoy attacked on the airport road; two peacekeepers wounded
More than 25 people arrested by army intelligence, according to Interior Minister Ahmad al-Hajjar
President Aoun said the attackers 'will receive their punishment'

title: Disagreement with President Aoun over the central bank governor
description: On 27 March 2025 the cabinet appointed asset manager Karim Souaid as governor of the Banque du Liban, the first permanent governor since Riad Salameh's term ended in 2023, by 17 votes out of 24. Salam voted against: he said he had 'voiced reservations over his appointment, along with a number of ministers' for 'a host of reasons', including 'keenness on protecting depositors' rights and preserving the state's assets', and said any governor must follow the government's policy of a new IMF programme, bank restructuring and protection of depositors. Naharnet reported a clash between Salam and President Joseph Aoun, who backed Souaid, ahead of the vote; critics quoted by Al Jazeera questioned Souaid's ties to the banking sector.
key_facts: 27 March 2025: Souaid appointed with 17 of 24 votes; Salam and several ministers opposed
Salam: 'The governor … must commit from today to the financial policies of our reformist government'
In 2026 the central bank and the government continued to differ over the bank resolution law

title: Cabinet decisions on Hezbollah's weapons and walkouts by Shiite ministers
description: On 5 August 2025, under heavy US pressure according to AP and amid fears of intensified Israeli strikes, the cabinet tasked the army with a plan to confine weapons to state forces by the end of 2025; the Amal and Hezbollah ministers present walked out. Hezbollah said the Salam government had 'committed a grave sin', that the decision 'fully serves Israel's interest' and that it would 'deal with it as if it does not exist', and its leader Naim Qassem said the group would not disarm while Israeli attacks continued. On 5 September 2025 all five Shiite ministers, including the independent Fadi Makki, walked out when the army commander presented his plan, which the cabinet 'welcomed'; they did not resign. Salam said in late August that the path of monopolising arms 'has begun and there is no turning back'. Hezbollah is designated a terrorist organisation by the US and several other states; the EU lists its military wing.
key_facts: 5 August 2025: army tasked with a plan; Environment Minister Tamara al-Zein (Amal) and Health Minister Rakan Nassereddine (Hezbollah) walk out
6 August 2025: Hezbollah calls the decision a 'grave sin'
5 September 2025: five Shiite ministers walk out; the cabinet keeps the plan's details confidential and asks for monthly reports
Hezbollah and Amal ministers stayed in the government

title: Hezbollah defies a ban on projecting images onto Raouché Rock
description: On 25 September 2025, at a commemoration of the killing of Hezbollah leaders Hassan Nasrallah and Hashem Safieddine, supporters projected their portraits onto Beirut's Raouché Rock, although the Beirut governor's permit for the gathering explicitly barred illuminating the landmark; security forces did not intervene. Salam called it 'a clear violation' and a 'new lapse' by the organisers, cancelled his appointments the next day to follow the case, and instructed the interior, justice and defence ministers to arrest and prosecute those responsible. Hezbollah supporters ran a campaign of insults against him on social media.
key_facts: The permit capped attendance at 500 and banned lighting the rock from land, sea or air
26 September 2025: emergency ministerial meeting at the Grand Serail condemns 'a clear breach of the permit'
Cassation public prosecutor Jamal Hajjar issued search and investigation notices against two individuals over the projection

title: Opposition to the 'financial gap' bill on depositors' losses
description: The draft law approved by the cabinet on 26 December 2025, by 13 votes to 9, allocates the losses of the 2019 financial collapse between the state, the central bank, commercial banks and depositors. Banking officials said it placed too heavy a burden on banks, while a lawyer for the Depositors Union told Al Jazeera it let banks 'off fairly easily' and shifted most of the burden to the state, adding that the IMF itself asked 'how can you make depositors pay before bankers?'. Salam defended the bill as 'not ideal' but 'a realistic and fair step on the path to restoring rights'.
key_facts: 26 December 2025: bill approved 13–9 and sent to parliament
Deposits up to $100,000 to be repaid over four years; larger balances partly in bonds backed by central-bank assets
September 2026: the bill is still pending; the Finance Minister says an IMF programme depends on it

title: Expatriate-vote dispute and the two-year postponement of the parliamentary election
description: Ahead of the May 2026 election, Salam's government and the Lebanese Forces-led camp wanted expatriates to vote for all 128 MPs in their home districts, while Speaker Nabih Berri refused to put the amendment on parliament's agenda, leaving the 2017 law's six seats for a diaspora constituency unimplemented; Salam said in February 2026 that the issue required legislation and that only parliament could postpone the election. After the war began, parliament voted on 9 March 2026, by 76 to 41 with four abstentions, to extend its term by two years to 31 May 2028, on a proposal put forward by Berri. The Lebanese Forces, the Free Patriotic Movement, the Kataeb and others had sought a shorter delay; Michel Moawad called the vote a 'massacre … against democracy and the Constitution', and several blocs appealed to the Constitutional Council. Analysts at the Carnegie Endowment noted the extended parliament will elect the next president.
key_facts: February 2026: Salam says the government is ready to hold elections on schedule
9 March 2026: two-year extension adopted 76–41
11 March 2026: appeals filed with the Constitutional Council

title: Ban on Hezbollah's military activities as the 2026 war begins
description: On 2 March 2026 Hezbollah fired rockets and drones at Israel, saying it was avenging the killing of Iran's supreme leader Ali Khamenei in the US–Israeli strikes two days earlier. Israel responded with massive airstrikes and a ground invasion. After an emergency cabinet meeting, Salam announced 'the immediate prohibition of all of Hezbollah's security and military activities, considering them to be outside the law', ordered the army to prevent launches from Lebanese territory, and asked the US and France to obtain a halt to Israeli attacks; according to a source close to the government, two Amal ministers and one Hezbollah minister approved the decision. Salam later told Asharq Al-Awsat that Lebanon could have avoided the conflict 'were it not for the strategic error committed by Hezbollah'. According to Lebanese authorities, more than 4,300 people had been killed in Lebanon by Israeli attacks by September 2026. The government also imposed visas on Iranian visitors, which Salam attributed to intelligence on Revolutionary Guards operations that could harm Lebanon's security.
key_facts: 2 March 2026: cabinet bans Hezbollah's military and security activity and orders it to hand over its weapons
Salam asks the ceasefire guarantors, the US and France, to obtain an end to Israeli attacks on all Lebanese territory
March 2026: Salam tells Asharq Al-Awsat the war was a 'catastrophe' caused by Hezbollah's 'strategic error'
Casualty figures are those of the Lebanese authorities, as reported by AFP in September 2026

title: Expulsion of Iran's ambassador, who refused to leave
description: On 24 March 2026 the Foreign Ministry, under Minister Youssef Raggi, withdrew its approval of Iran's ambassador Mohammad Reza Sheibani, declared him persona non grata and ordered him to leave by 29 March, citing 'Tehran's violation of diplomatic norms', after Beirut accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of commanding Hezbollah's operations in the war; Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar welcomed the decision. Hezbollah and Amal opposed the decision, and their four ministers boycotted a cabinet session in protest. Sheibani remained in Beirut and in August 2026 General Security granted him a six-month residency permit 'on a normal basis', which Raggi said violated 'a final and binding sovereign decision by the Lebanese state'.
key_facts: 24 March 2026: accreditation withdrawn; Lebanon's ambassador to Iran summoned
Hezbollah and Amal ministers boycott a cabinet session in protest (AFP)
August 2026: Sheibani granted a six-month residency permit as a civilian resident

title: Direct negotiations with Israel and the June 2026 framework agreement
description: Salam's government took part in direct talks with Israel that began in Washington on 14 April 2026, described by Al Jazeera as the first direct negotiations between the two states since 1983, and led to a framework agreement signed on 26 June 2026 by the two countries' ambassadors in the presence of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. It links a phased Israeli withdrawal, starting with 'pilot zones', to the disarmament of Hezbollah and provides for working groups towards a peace and security agreement; Salam has presented it as the path to 'the complete Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory'. Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem called it 'humiliating, shameful and a surrender of sovereignty' and said the government was legitimising Israel's occupation; Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah said enforcing it by force would lead to 'civil war'. Hezbollah supporters blocked the airport road on the night of the signing. Israeli officials have said further withdrawals depend on results, not a timetable. In September 2026 Salam asked Washington for a clear timetable and a verification mechanism.
key_facts: 14 April 2026: first round of direct talks in Washington
26 June 2026: framework agreement signed at the State Department
27 June 2026: Hezbollah rejects the agreement; a prosecutor orders security forces to prevent riots
28 September 2026: Israel has withdrawn from one of three pilot zones

title: Seizure of an explosives truck at Dahr al-Baidar
description: In early October 2026 (5 October according to L'Orient-Le Jour, 8 October according to AFP) security forces stopped a vehicle heading to Beirut at the Dahr al-Baidar checkpoint on the Bekaa–Beirut highway carrying 780 kg of explosives, including 250 kg of TNT and 250 kg of C4, according to judicial officials quoted by AP; the two men arrested admitted belonging to Hezbollah, according to a judicial source cited by Asharq Al-Awsat. Salam called it a 'criminal operation' and said the government would pursue 'all those involved … and those behind them'. Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah said the explosives belonged to the group and were intended for use against Israel, and demanded their return and the release of those arrested. Justice Minister Adel Nassar proposed referring the case to the Judicial Council, the special court for crimes against state security; on 20 October a judge summoned two Hezbollah officials for questioning, and Hezbollah MPs accused Salam of submitting to foreign 'dictates' after he called for the arrest of all those involved in possessing and transporting illegal weapons. Salam is not a party to the case, which is at the investigation stage. Those arrested and summoned are presumed innocent.
key_facts: 780 kg of explosives seized at the Dahr al-Baidar checkpoint; two suspected Hezbollah members arrested
Hezbollah acknowledges ownership through MP Hassan Fadlallah
20 October 2026: judicial summonses for two Hezbollah officials (AFP)
Proposed referral to the Judicial Council not decided by the cabinet as of 22 October 2026
